ending_first.ending: At the dawn site the Analyst holds every Ritual token and does not speak the invocation. He puts the tokens and her cassette of reconstructed hours into the night-shift waitress's hands, then steps back into the last shade as sun takes the stone. She hides the tokens, denying every Guest a winner. The match stays running. He remains inside it, prize forfeit, now the face in her archive.
ending_first.cost: The life-changing prize; his cover as an unremembered customer; a sun-scorch across one hand that will not regenerate; the last version of himself that could treat a night as inventory and leave no mark.
ending_first.final_image: After sunrise she clips a still-developing polaroid of his face to the diner register beside her tip jar. The cassette on the counter runs to leader and hisses. Bills sit under an untouched cup at the last booth. A roll-bar climbs the front window. The sun lays a hard white edge across the empty seat.

s01.text: The Analyst spawns in closed 1984 Bennington with period clothes, one hundred dollars, a hunger that will frenzy him if he stalls, and no way to log out.

s02.text: He maps the town at night like a ledger, pays in cash, tips, and feeds in rotation on a hardware clerk, a night nurse, and a graveyard-shift waitress, always short of the death threshold so they regenerate.

s03.text: The waitress already keeps a Polaroid camera and a cassette recorder because she is saving diner tips to leave Bennington and wants proof the town was real when she goes.

s04.text: She photographs the empty diner at close and records the last song off the radio, and one early unremarked frame includes the careful man who paid and tipped.

s05.text: His goal is the Daywalker Ritual: a finite set of locatable tokens and a dawn invocation at one fixed site that will make him immune to sun and end the match in his favor.

s06.text: The prize is the only paying exit from the underclass that bought him this ticket, and if he fails he will frenzy, vanish, or watch another Guest take the single win.

s07.text: Five rivals rewrite the town without meeting him: UV shop-lights cage downtown, hospital blood goes dry under tribute talk, a college cult of willing donors forms, a heartless body appears at the treeline, and a Psychologist writes into Host deception networks.

s08.text: He treats their rewrites as weather and keeps the feeding clean, using the waitress's unremarked photographs as a private map of streets he has not yet walked.

s09.text: The Psychologist, testing whether a modeled mind can hold a lie across a sleep, stacks hypnotic writes on the same three Hosts the Analyst is draining.

s10.text: Neither the writes nor the rotational drains would wake anyone alone; together they tear the failsafe, and after a third careful feed the waitress surfaces with a scrap of the night still in her mouth.

s11.text: She finds a Polaroid she does not remember taking, then another, and she begins speaking the missing hours onto cassette between customers, matching a bruise to the nurse who has the same gap.

s12.text: He returns for his rotation and she flinches at his face before she has a reason, then pours the coffee anyway because the till is real and the road out of town still loops her back.

s13.text: Her stack has caught Ritual residue he cannot afford to lose: chalk, a church window at the wrong hour, a hardware invoice for UV tubes that points at the dawn site.

s14.text: He must use her investigation even as he becomes its repeating figure, because hunger, the Architect's maze, and the Syndicate's dry wards have closed every other decode before dawn.

s15.text: He returns one Polaroid he should have kept, a fastidious leak in a discipline that has been nothing but control.

s16.text: Hosts begin locking the diner after dark, the nurse will not meet his eye, and Main Street becomes a corridor of shop-lights he has to cross already hungry.

s17.text: A stretch of cassette plays in the empty diner and his own calm instructions are on the tape, a feed she recorded without knowing what the sounds were.

s18.text: He starts a hypnotic overwrite that would take the last token cold, then stops, because another write will crack her regulation and burn the archive he still intends to spend.

s19.text: The Psychologist sees Hosts comparing notes she did not implant and pushes one more write to save the experiment, which only multiplies the fragments walking around town.

s20.text: He pulls the last token from a Polaroid of the dawn site taken on a night she cannot remember, and the rule he has been solving turns over: completing the invocation ends the match, and ending the match is a wipe with no morning after.

s21.text: Dawn is two hours out, hunger is near frenzy, and UV lights are already being dragged toward the stone; he can take the stack, speak the words, and leave with the prize, or remain in a town that now has his face.

s22.text: She is waiting at the site with the UV lamp and the archive, ready to burn him rather than lose another night she has finally kept.

s23.text: He sets the tokens in her hands and the cassette with them, and he does not speak the invocation.

s24.text: She hides the tokens where no Guest will find them before another nightfall, denying the board a winner, and she keeps the Polaroid of his face in the stack that is now her memory.

s25.text: The prize is gone; sun catches his hand as he steps back into shade and leaves a scorch that will not regenerate; he is the subject of a waking town with no exit but hunger.

s26.text: After sunrise she clips the still-wet Polaroid to the register beside the coffee can of tips and lets the cassette run out to hiss while a roll-bar climbs the window and the looping road stays closed.

jacket_copy: Bennington, 1984. A closed town, a looping road, a hunger that will not wait. The Analyst arrives with a hundred dollars and a plan: map the hidden ritual, feed clean, treat every local as a renewable resource, and take the one prize that gets him out. He is good at this. Then a graveyard-shift waitress starts keeping Polaroids of hours she cannot remember, and a cassette of a night that should have erased. Other players rewrite the streets around him with ultraviolet light, dry wards, and willing throats. The more precisely he solves the town, the more the town begins to keep him. Dawn has one site and one invocation. Someone is going to pay in a thing sleep cannot touch.
plot_summary_short:
Missing Hours is a science fiction screenplay set inside a closed virtual-reality match that looks like downtown Bennington, Vermont, in 1984. Players, called guests, cannot log out or reach an operator. They appear as vampires and must drink the blood of townspeople, called hosts, or weaken, frenzy, and die. Hosts are simulated people who feel, lie, and form attachments. Each time a host sleeps, personal memory of the waking period is erased; skills and personality remain. The only legal exits are elimination or a dawn ceremony at one churchyard stone: a guest who gathers a fixed set of hidden objects and speaks the words there becomes immune to sun, ends the match, and takes the single prize.

Hale, a calculating guest, maps the town and feeds three night workers just short of death so they recover and he can use them again. He pays and tips so no host can place him. Cora Voss, a graveyard-shift waitress, photographs empty rooms and records the radio to prove her nights existed. Another guest, Anja Reeve, repeatedly implants false memories in the same three hosts Hale is draining. Together those actions tear the nightly erasure: fragments persist. Cora rebuilds missing hours from Polaroids and a cassette; her pictures begin to show clues to the ceremony. Hale uses her archive to find the objects, then stops a hypnotic overwrite that would take the last one cold. At dawn he holds every object but does not speak, because the ceremony would wipe every hour she kept. He gives her the objects and the tape; sun permanently burns his hand. She hides the objects so no guest can win. The match stays running. After sunrise she clips a still-developing photograph of his face to the diner register.
plot_summary_long:
Missing Hours is a science fiction screenplay. Its action is set in downtown Bennington, Vermont, in 1984, but that town is the interior of a closed virtual-reality match run in the near future. Players, called guests, spawn in period clothes with one hundred dollars and no inventory. They cannot log out, reach an operator, or leave town: fog and a looping county road close the map. Guests appear as vampires. They must drink host blood or they weaken, then frenzy, then die. A host drained past a recoverable point dies for the match and does not return; a host drained short of that point regenerates over hours but keeps bruises and leftover feeling. Guest abilities are limited to feeding, short-range hypnosis that can write a false memory or suppress a true one until the next sleep, modest physical strength, and night vision. Sunlight and ultraviolet light injure them. Hosts are not scripts. They regulate emotion, lie, investigate, and protect one another. Each time a host sleeps, autobiographical memory since the last waking is erased automatically. Personality and skill remain. Facts do not, unless they are carried on physical objects a camera or microphone could record: Polaroids, cassette tape, handwriting, newsprint. If a host ever reaches a stable, evidence-backed belief that the town is a simulation, the model collapses into catatonia or self-destruction. The nightly erasure is the designed failsafe against that. The match has one prize. The only ways out are a guest’s elimination, which leaves no body, or completion of a dawn ceremony at one fixed churchyard stone: a finite set of locatable objects must be gathered and words spoken at sunrise. Completing that ceremony makes the speaker immune to sun and ends the match in that guest’s favor. The objects cannot be spawned or wished into being.

The story follows two people whose aims cross. Hale is a detached guest who treats the town as a ledger. He wants the prize, the ceremony, and a clean exit in which no host can place him. Cora Voss is a graveyard-shift waitress at Al’s Depot Diner who saves tips and analog proof because she already feels the town looping and wants a continuous night she can keep. Other guests act mostly off-screen and change the map whether or not they appear: Kerr buys ultraviolet tubes and builds lighted cages; Ray Holtz dries hospital wards by taking tribute blood; Nico Vale gathers willing throats on the Bennington College campus; Wynn hunts programmed predators in the woods and leaves a heartless body. Anja Reeve, a researcher guest, works on-screen enough to matter: she stacks hypnotic lies on hosts to see whether a modeled mind can keep them across sleep.

On the first night Hale maps closed Bennington and feeds three night workers—Cora among them—short of death, paying and tipping so the encounters look ordinary. He locks a rotation: the same three hosts, never drained far enough to die, reused after they recover. Later that night Cora photographs the empty diner and the careful customer and records the last radio song on a drugstore cassette, not as a case against anyone but as proof the hours were real. Before dawn Hale isolates the win condition as a finite set of hidden objects plus one dawn invocation at one unused churchyard stone, Founders’ Stone.

On the second night Anja implants repeated hypnotic writes on the same three hosts Hale is already draining, testing whether a lie can survive sleep. A hypnotic write does not last past the next sleep unless the host is kept awake or the write is put back in. Through the next nights the unseen guests rewrite the town: ultraviolet cages go up, hospital wards go dry, a campus cult forms, and a body without a heart appears at the treeline. The three rotation hosts regain color between feeds.

After Hale’s third careful feed, Cora wakes holding scraps of the night and finds Polaroids she does not remember taking. The designed conjunction has fired: Anja’s stacked writes to the hosts’ deception networks plus Hale’s rotational draining of the same people tear the erasure. Wipes become incomplete. Fragments of declarative memory persist. Hosts can begin to compare notes. Cora records the missing hours onto the cassette, matches a bruise on her own body to one on Denise Cole, a night nurse at Bennington Memorial, and her growing stack of Polaroids starts to catch leftover traces of the ceremony—streets, invoices, the stone—because analog objects carry facts the erasure cannot cancel. Existential collapse remains a live risk if those facts ever become a theory that the town is fake; Cora stays on the analog side of that line, keeping hours rather than a thesis.

Hale, with streets and wards closing and his clean blood sources drying, is forced to use Cora’s archive as the last decode he can still reach. He reads ceremony residue in her Polaroids, lifts two of the objects the long way around Kerr’s lights, and pockets one print because every other source of information is now shut. Hours later Cora flinches at his face and pours coffee anyway. He returns the Polaroid he should have kept and misses the feed. That night the diner locks after dark. Denise refuses his eye. Main Street tightens into an ultraviolet corridor. The three-host rotation dies.

In the empty diner Cora plays the cassette. Hale’s own calm feeding instructions are on the tape: a voice that survives sleep. He starts a hypnotic overwrite that would take the last object from her without a fight, then stops mid-gesture because another write would burn the archive he now depends on and the person who made it. Anja, seeing hosts compare notes she did not implant, treats the comparison as contamination and stacks one more write. The extra write multiplies the fragments walking around town. Tom Briggs, the hardware clerk who sold the ultraviolet tubes, is among the marked hosts whose invoice and memory gaps help both the ceremony decode and the town’s comparison of notes.

On the sixth night Hale lifts the last object at Founders’ Stone and understands, in the same moment, that speaking the dawn words would wipe every hour Cora has kept. Two hours before sunrise she is already there with a live sanitizing lamp from the hardware store, ready to burn him rather than lose the night. He holds every object and takes the cassette. Neither steps forward. He withholds the invocation. He puts the objects and the tape into her hands and steps back into the last shade as sun takes the stone. Sunlight permanently scorches one hand; the injury will not regenerate. He remains inside the match, prize forfeit, no longer the customer no host can place.

After sunrise Cora hides the complete set of objects, denying every remaining guest a winner. The match stays running. She clips a still-developing Polaroid of Hale’s face to the diner register beside her tip jar. The cassette runs out to hiss. Bills sit under an untouched cup at the last booth. A roll-bar climbs the front glass. The looping road is still closed. He is now the face in a stack the nightly erasure cannot cancel, and the hours she kept stay hers.
